title: 911 tape shows man's state of mind before he died in police custody
subtitle: Derrick Madrusan's death ruled as cocaine overdose: coroner's jury
article: A 911 tape obtained by CBC News sheds new light on the events leading up to the death of a Kelowna, B.C., man while in police custody in June 2006. Derrick Madrusan, 39, died minutes after he was subdued and hog-tied by four RCMP officers.

The 911 tape shows clearly that Madrusan was in a delusional state at the time of his arrest and 911 operators could hear Juliana Verona screaming as her son, Madrusan, tried to tie her up with a sheet.
The 911 tape also shows Madrusan believed something was coming to harm his parentsand his bizarre actions were aimed at protecting them.
"Don't put that on top of me! We're OK, Derrick!" Juliana Verona responds, as the tape picks up the conversation between Madrusan and his mother.

A coroner's jury concluded on Wednesday that Madrusan's death was an accidental cocaine overdose, but it included a recommendation for the RCMP that psychotic suspects must be watched by an RCMP officer until medical help arrives.

The coroner's jury found the actions of police had nothing to do with Madrusan's death. It found Madrusan had gone into a drug-induced psychotic state and then suffered a fatal heart attack. Pathologist Dr. Bill Currie said such deaths are common for someone suffering from drug psychosis.

"They are generally at risk, and if they get a very high body temperature they can often lead to fatal cardiac results, and they're very difficult to resuscitate," Currie said. Madrusan was left alone in the back of a police car after his arrest. The jury recommended at least one RCMP officer should stay with a psychotic suspect until medical help arrives.

"They [psychotic suspects] should probably be watched closely because when they go into this phase when they stop suddenly all of the noise, and they become very quiet, that's usually an indication that something terrible has happened, and their heart has suddenly stopped beating," Currie said.
